intro: One planet, four views. Drag the date through the year and watch the noon sun climb and fall at your latitude; follow a weather balloon from the equator to the pole through the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells; send ocean air over a mountain and watch a rain shadow form; then switch the Pacific between La Niña and El Niño and compare them side by side.
howItWorks:
Sun and seasons. The latitude where the noon sun is overhead (the declination) is 23.44° × sin(360° × (284 + day) / 365), the standard approximation (Cooper, 1969). The noon sun angle is 90° minus the degrees between your latitude and that latitude. Day length is 24/π × arccos(−tan(latitude) × tan(declination)) hours. Daily sunlight is the average over 24 hours on level ground at the top of the atmosphere, from a solar constant of 1,361 W/m² (NASA) at the average Earth-sun distance. In the side view the axis is drawn tilted toward the sun by the declination, so the overhead sun always lands on the right latitude.

Winds. Three cells in each hemisphere with their edges at about 0°, 30° and 60°: air rises near the equator and 60° (wet belts) and sinks near 30° and the poles (dry belts); surface winds are bent right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern by Earth's rotation (NOAA JetStream).

Rain shadow. A parcel of air cools 10 °C per km while it is dry and about 6 °C per km inside a cloud, and warms 10 °C per km as it sinks (the dry and typical moist adiabatic rates, rounded as the course uses them). The cloud base comes from the dew point: about 125 m per °C between the air temperature and its dew point.

El Niño and La Niña. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center calls El Niño when the 3-month average sea surface temperature anomaly in the Niño 3.4 region is +0.5 °C or more, and La Niña at −0.5 °C or less. The cross-section is a sketch: trade wind strength, the thermocline's depth and the upwelling change with the anomaly in the direction the observations show, but the sizes are illustrative, not measured.
